title: 02:14 — the checklist, not the scramble
spec: M26 · detect, decide, act, verify, remediate, communicate
intro: The auto-deny alert fires at 02:14. RUNBOOK_auto_deny_spike is six ordered steps and an escalation ladder, and following it puts the pipeline back in band eleven minutes later. The same incident without a runbook took three hours and forty minutes last quarter.

provenance.source: a narrated 2am prior-auth incident executed against M26's RUNBOOK_auto_deny_spike; timestamps, rates and counts are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: This walks M26's A Runbook as Executable Checklist — the six Step() entries of RUNBOOK_auto_deny_spike and its escalation list, in the order they actually run.

steps.title: Detect and decide — 02:14 to 02:18
narrative: The page reads alert:auto_deny_rate > baseline + 0.05. Actual is 0.214 against a baseline of 0.081, so it is +0.133 — nearly three times the alert threshold. The on-call engineer has been awake for ninety seconds.

Step one is detect, and its content is a single instruction: confirm the spike on dashboards/pa, not a data artifact. Three minutes go into checking that request volume is normal, that no upstream feed re-delivered a batch, and that the metric is not a broken rollup. It is real.

Step two is decide, and the runbook decides for you: if sustained >10m -> rollback; else investigate. The rate has been above the line since 02:04, so that is ten minutes and the branch is settled. Severity is SEV1, which auto-pages the senior engineer. Nobody at 2am is being asked to weigh anything.
steps.youDo: Open your own top alert and read what it tells the responder to do next. If the answer is 'look at the dashboard', you have a detector, not a runbook.
steps.claudeSays: The decide step is a rule with a threshold and a clock, not a judgement call. That is deliberate: the responder is tired, and the rule is not.

terminal.text:
step 1 detect     confirm spike on dashboards/pa, not a data artifact
step 2 decide     if sustained >10m -> rollback; else investigate
step 3 act        emergency_rollback("auto-deny spike")
step 4 verify     auto_deny_rate back to baseline within 10m
step 5 remediate  reexamine_since(incident_start)
step 6 communicate medical_director, compliance, status_page
02:17:22  volume 5,020/hr (normal)  no batch re-delivery  rollup healthy  -> spike is real
02:18:05  sustained since 02:04 = 14m > 10m  -> branch: ROLLBACK. senior_eng paged (SEV1)

after.title: THE DECISION, MADE BY THE RULE

steps.title: Act — 02:19, one command
narrative: Step three is emergency_rollback("auto-deny spike"). It is the M11 procedure, already written, already rehearsed, and reachable from the runbook as a callable — not as a paragraph describing what to do.

That distinction is the module in miniature. A prose runbook says revert to the last known-good bundle, and at 2am the responder then has to remember which registry, which flag name, and whether the flag is per-region. An executable step calls the function that knows all three.
Flag flip to the v7 fingerprint: 6.1 seconds across 42 workers. No build, no deploy, no restart.
steps.claudeSays: The runbook did not describe the rollback. It invoked it. The description would have been the lossy copy.
steps.youDo: Take the longest prose step in your own runbook and replace it with a function call. The step should say what and why; the code should hold the how, because the how goes stale silently.

before.title: BEFORE — the prose version of this step

view.text: "If the auto-deny rate is elevated, revert the prompt bundle to the previous known-good version using the feature flag system, then confirm the change has propagated." — correct, unrunnable, and it does not name the registry, the flag, or the fingerprint. Last quarter it also named a flag that had since been renamed.

steps.title: Verify and remediate — 02:25 to 02:31
narrative: Step four names the metric that has to move: auto_deny_rate back to baseline within 10m. At 02:25 it reads 0.084, inside the band. If it had not, the runbook would have escalated rather than declaring victory — a verify step with no failure branch is decoration.

Step five is the one that makes this a real runbook: reexamine_since(incident_start). The bad bundle went live at 02:04 and was reverted at 02:19, fifteen minutes at 5,000 determinations an hour — 1,250 determinations to re-adjudicate on v7.

166 of them come back with a different decision. That is the excess deny rate of 13.3 points applied to 1,250, and it matches: those are members who were denied by a bundle that no longer exists. They get reopened and notified.
steps.claudeSays: Verify closes the incident for future traffic. Remediate closes it for the traffic that already went through. The runbook has both because a rollback without the second one leaves 166 wrong denials behind.
steps.youDo: Count the steps in your runbook that run after the metric recovers. Zero is the common answer and it is the expensive one.

terminal.text: Step("verify", check="auto_deny_rate back to baseline within 10m")
verify PASS  0.084 within baseline band  recovered 6m12s after act
02:31  166 determinations changed decision (deny -> approve) -> reopened and notified

items.label: after act (02:25)
items.note: in band, 6m12s after the flag flip

steps.title: Communicate, and the ladder that made it eleven minutes
narrative: Step six notifies medical_director, compliance, and the status page — in that order, with the 166 reopened cases attached. Clinical impact means the medical director is not a courtesy copy; they are the person who decides whether the reopened determinations need individual review.

The escalation ladder ran alongside all of it: oncall_eng at 02:14, senior_eng automatically at 02:18 when the severity resolved to SEV1, medical_director at 02:31 when clinical impact was quantified. Nobody had to decide who to wake up, which is exactly the decision people get wrong at 2am.

Total time from page to in-band: eleven minutes. The same failure mode last quarter, before this runbook existed, ran three hours and forty minutes — most of it spent finding the flag name and arguing about whether to roll forward instead. The runbook did not make anyone smarter. It removed the four decisions that a tired person makes badly.
steps.claudeSays: Six steps executed in order, each one either a check with a branch or a call with a result. The prose version of this document could not have been executed at all — only interpreted.
steps.youDo: After your next incident, diff what the responder actually did against what the runbook said. Every gap is a step that was improvised, and improvised steps are where the minutes go.

cells: no detect step; checked six dashboards
no decide rule; the hotfix was tried first
the wiki page named a flag renamed in June
nobody knew it was a step

views.text: 3h40m to 11m, and the difference is not skill — it is that four decisions were made in advance, in daylight, by people who were not tired. Keep the runbook executable so it cannot silently name a renamed flag, rehearse it on a game day, and update it from every postmortem. A runbook nobody has run since it was written is a document, and documents rot.
